reader.title: Whipping death of Liddell at Sugar Hill camp
bases: Liddell died in custody as a convict after a whipping by the camp's deputy warden, J. W. Tierce, a single official acting on a prisoner (A1, A12, A15).

The coroner's verdict and jury held that Liddell died from a whipping by one deputy warden, though the state warden reported natural causes (A1, A6, A15); no group of three or more and no crowd is reported, and no reason for the whipping is given (A12, A15).
The coroner's verdict and the coroner's jury held that Liddell died after the whipping (A1, A12, A15, A17), while State Warden Moore reported that he died from natural causes (A6).

summary.text: The whipping death of Liddell at Sugar Hill camp was the death in August 1905 of a Black convict at a labor camp in Bartow County, Georgia, after a whipping by the camp's deputy warden, J. W. Tierce.

A county coroner's verdict that Liddell had been whipped to death led the state prison commission to suspend Tierce, but State Warden J. C. Moore reported after his own inquiry that the prisoner had died of natural causes.
A coroner's jury at Cartersville then held Tierce under $5,000 bond for manslaughter and rebuked Moore, a sequence carried by white papers across the South and by the Savannah Tribune.
Liddell, whose first name does not appear in the coverage, was a convict "being worked" at Sugar Hill camp in Bartow County, which an Atlanta dispatch said was operated by Joel Hurt of Atlanta.
Tierce was the deputy warden at the camp, and a Dr. Vaughan served as its physician.
At the request of the Bartow County commissioners, the county coroner investigated Liddell's death and returned a verdict that he had been whipped to death.

When word reached the prison commission in Atlanta on August 12, its secretary, Goodloe Yancey, suspended Tierce and ordered a full investigation, and State Warden Moore made "a hurried trip" to the camp.
Moore returned from Cartersville on August 14 and, according to an Atlanta dispatch, reported that he had made "a very careful investigation" and found that the prisoner died from natural causes.

Rejecting the warden's finding, the coroner's jury at Cartersville held Tierce under $5,000 bond for manslaughter and also placed Dr. Vaughan under bond "on account of alleged connection with the case."

The jury "severely criticises" Moore for his statement clearing Tierce of criminal responsibility, said he had not made much of an investigation, and called on him to name the physicians reported to have said that Liddell died from the bursting of a blood vessel.
The same Cartersville dispatch said that "the community is much stirred up over the affair."
No report of an indictment or trial of Tierce or Vaughan appears in the coverage through September 1905.

The first Associated Press dispatch from Atlanta ran on August 13 in the Washington Evening Star, the Montgomery Advertiser, the Newport News Daily Press, the Raleigh News & Observer and the Louisville Courier-Journal, and three days later in the Lancaster Ledger of South Carolina.

Its headlines, which did not give Liddell's race, made the coroner's verdict the news: "Convict Whipped to Death" in the Evening Star, with the subhead "Stir in Georgia Over Inhuman Treatment by Deputy Warden," and "Beaten to Death" in the Daily Press.

Moore's report followed on August 15 under headlines that took up his conclusion, such as "Was Not Whipped to Death" in the Birmingham Age-Herald and, two days later, "Did Not Whip Convict to Death" in the Caucasian of Clinton, North Carolina.
Weekly news columns in the Ceredo Advance of West Virginia and the Berea Citizen of Kentucky reduced the case to a two-sentence item on Tierce's suspension.

The coroner's jury reports, which called Liddell "the negro convict," reached fewer papers: the New York Evening World printed one under "Negro Whipped to Death" among short wire items, and the Gainesville Daily Sun ran "Guard Charged with Manslaughter."

The one Black-press report found, in the Savannah Tribune of August 19, put the story on its front page as "Warden Moore Criticised," with the subhead "Coroner's Jury Investigates Fatal Whipping of a Convict."
Its text condensed the same dispatch the Gainesville paper carried, without the jury's demand for the physicians' names, without naming Liddell's race and without comment.
The cause of Liddell's death was disputed between county and state officials.
The coroner and the coroner's jury held that he died from the whipping, while State Warden Moore reported natural causes and unnamed physicians were said to have blamed a burst blood vessel.
The jury's finding came from a local inquest and was made after Moore's report, which the jury said rested on little investigation.
Accounts also differ on Vaughan's bond, given as $300 by the Gainesville Daily Sun and $200 by the Savannah Tribune.

accounts.gist: At the county commissioners' request the coroner investigated and returned a verdict that Liddell had been whipped to death.

accounts.label: State Warden Moore
accounts.gist: After what the dispatch called a very careful investigation, Moore reported that the prisoner died from natural causes.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: The jury held Tierce for manslaughter and the camp physician on bond, said Moore had made little investigation, and demanded the names of physicians reported to blame a burst blood vessel.

framing.detail: The first wire ran under 'Convict Whipped to Death' with the Evening Star subhead 'Stir in Georgia Over Inhuman Treatment by Deputy Warden', without naming Liddell's race.
Moore's report ran under headlines adopting his conclusion: 'Was Not Whipped to Death', 'Did Not Whip Convict to Death'.
Jury reports called Liddell 'the negro convict' under 'Negro Whipped to Death' and 'Guard Charged with Manslaughter'.
The Savannah Tribune put the jury report on page one as 'Warden Moore Criticised', subhead 'Coroner's Jury Investigates Fatal Whipping of a Convict', without comment and without naming race.
